title: Emergency medicine — hypoglycemia authoring examples
description: Two fictional adult hypoglycemia cases: a cooperative patient after a missed meal and a more severe activity-associated presentation with unsafe swallowing and recurrence risk. Partially checked against the listed guidance; qualified clinician and local-protocol review are required before teaching.

The pair shows autonomic symptoms, confusion and severe impaired responsiveness.
The cases teach bedside glucose as an immediate investigation but do not provide a full cause-directed investigation workup.
The severe presentation and recurrence/prolonged-event risk are addressed, but the wider complication spectrum is not assessed.
The pair covers ED priorities, route selection and reassessment without doses, rescue algorithms or local prescribing protocols.
The pair distinguishes monitored discharge consideration from admission for recurrence risk; it does not replace local disposition policy.

cases.title: Confusion after a missed meal
learningObjectives: Recognize common clinical features of acute hypoglycemia and confirm it with a bedside measurement.
Prioritize emergency assessment and select a treatment route that matches the patient’s ability to swallow safely.
Reassess the clinical and glucose response, identify recurrence risk and plan an appropriate disposition.

criticalActionGroups.label: Correct the low glucose using a route appropriate to the examination

demographics.context: Brought to the ED by a companion after developing symptoms at work.

initialPresentation.complaint: Sweating, tremor and confusion after missing a meal.
initialPresentation.appearance: Awake and responding to questions, but sweaty, shaky and mildly confused.
initialPresentation.condition: Awake with autonomic symptoms and mild confusion.

steps.prompt: A patient with an acute change in behavior and sweating arrives at the ED. What should happen first?
steps.guidance: Start with immediate threats and reversible causes. Which rapid assessment can establish stability before non-urgent tasks?

actions.text: Perform an immediate ABCDE assessment
actions.feedback: ABCDE assessment establishes current stability and immediate priorities before a focused diagnostic plan. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: A rapid primary assessment is underway; immediate threats are addressed before non-urgent tasks.

patientChanges.condition: Awake and breathing spontaneously; rapid assessment is in progress.

actions.text: Wait without assessment or treatment
actions.feedback: An acute change in mental status can reflect a rapidly reversible emergency. Do not delay ABCDE assessment and bedside glucose for a full history or routine imaging. [R1]
actions.consequence: No primary assessment or corrective treatment has started; the patient remains symptomatic.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the immediate plan
actions.feedback: No specific immediate action was identified. State an actionable primary assessment before non-urgent tasks. [R1]
actions.consequence: No new assessment or treatment is started; the patient remains in the current condition.

steps.prompt: The primary assessment is underway. Which immediately available result could change what you do next?
steps.guidance: Choose a rapid bedside investigation for a reversible cause of altered behavior. Avoid tests that do not address the immediate threat.

actions.text: Check a bedside capillary glucose
actions.feedback: The measured glucose of 2.4 mmol/L is below the hypoglycemia alert threshold and requires prompt correction; do not delay treatment for a laboratory confirmation. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The bedside meter returns an immediate result.

actions.text: Arrange routine head CT before checking bedside glucose
actions.feedback: There is no trauma or focal finding in the initial presentation to justify delaying a rapid glucose check. If symptoms persist after correction or new findings emerge, assess for other causes. [R1]
actions.consequence: No new glucose result is available; the patient remains symptomatic.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the investigation plan
actions.feedback: No specific immediate investigation was identified. State which bedside result could rapidly change care. [R1]
actions.consequence: No new investigation result is available; the patient remains in the current condition.

steps.prompt: The low bedside glucose is confirmed. What focused examination finding is needed before choosing a treatment route?
steps.guidance: Treatment safety depends on current mental status and ability to protect the airway and swallow, not simply on whether the patient is awake.

actions.text: Assess airway, mental status and ability to swallow safely
actions.feedback: The examination establishes whether oral treatment is safe and whether airway support or a parenteral route is needed. Being awake alone does not establish safe swallowing. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: A focused airway, neurologic and swallow-safety assessment is completed.

reveals.label: Focused findings
reveals.text: Airway patent; follows commands, handles secretions and swallows safely. No vomiting, seizure, trauma or focal neurological deficit.

actions.text: Assume swallowing is safe because the patient is awake
actions.feedback: Wakefulness alone does not establish safe swallowing. Confirm the patient can cooperate and protect the airway before oral treatment. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: Swallow safety has not been established; no examination result is available.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the examination plan
actions.feedback: No focused examination was identified. State how airway, mental status and swallow safety will be assessed before choosing a route. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No new examination finding is available; the patient remains in the current condition.

steps.prompt: The examination and glucose result are available. What treatment should be started now?
steps.guidance: Treat promptly with a route that is safe for the demonstrated level of consciousness and swallowing ability. Plan an objective reassessment.

actions.text: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate according to local protocol
actions.feedback: For a cooperative patient who can swallow safely, oral glucose-containing carbohydrate is the direct initial route. Recheck glucose and clinical status after treatment. [R2, R3]
actions.consequence: Oral carbohydrate is given; symptoms begin to settle, but no repeat measurement is available yet.

patientChanges.condition: Awake; sweating and tremor begin to ease.

actions.text: Give IV glucose according to local protocol
actions.feedback: IV glucose is an appropriate alternative when oral treatment cannot be taken or is unsafe; for this patient with demonstrated safe swallowing, oral carbohydrate is the direct initial route. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: IV glucose is administered; no repeat measurement is available yet.

patientChanges.condition: Awake; symptoms begin to ease after treatment.

actions.text: Give additional insulin to treat the low glucose
actions.feedback: Additional insulin can worsen hypoglycemia. Treat the low glucose first and review the active diabetes regimen after stabilization. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient remains symptomatic and the glucose may fall further.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the treatment plan
actions.feedback: No specific treatment was identified. State the treatment goal and a route appropriate to the examination. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No corrective treatment is started; the patient remains symptomatic.

steps.prompt: What should be checked after the initial treatment?
steps.guidance: Use both an objective glucose measurement and clinical response. A single improvement does not rule out recurrence.

actions.text: Repeat capillary glucose and reassess mental status after treatment
actions.feedback: A repeat bedside measurement and clinical reassessment confirm the initial response. Continue monitoring when the cause or medication profile creates recurrence risk. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The immediate glucose response is objectively checked.

reveals.label: Post-treatment reassessment
reveals.text: Glucose is 4.2 mmol/L (76 mg/dL). Alert and oriented; sweating and tremor have resolved.

patientChanges.condition: Alert and oriented; sweating and tremor have resolved.

actions.text: Assume correction because the patient looks better
actions.feedback: Symptom improvement alone is not enough to confirm biochemical correction. Repeat the glucose and reassess mental status. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The treatment response is not yet objectively confirmed.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the reassessment plan
actions.feedback: No specific reassessment was identified. State which objective measurement and clinical findings should be checked. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No new reassessment result is available; the patient remains under care.

steps.prompt: The immediate glucose response is known. What focused history will help explain the event and guide ongoing care?
steps.guidance: Ask briefly about medication, food intake, activity, prior episodes, illness and factors that could make hypoglycemia recur.

actions.text: Ask about diabetes medicines, recent doses, food intake, activity, prior episodes and relevant illness or kidney disease
actions.feedback: A short, targeted history identifies the likely trigger and medication-related recurrence risk without replacing stabilization or objective reassessment. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient and companion provide focused information about the event and medication history.

reveals.label: Event and intake
reveals.text: The usual rapid-acting mealtime insulin was taken before lunch, but the meal was then missed. No treatment was given before arrival.

reveals.label: Medication and recurrence factors
reveals.text: The patient took the usual rapid-acting mealtime insulin before lunch but then missed the meal. No sulfonylurea use, prior episode or known kidney disease is reported.

actions.text: Take a complete, non-targeted past history before identifying the event trigger
actions.feedback: Once immediate treatment and reassessment are underway, focus on the event, medicines, recent intake, activity and recurrence risks rather than allowing an unfocused interview to delay safe planning. [R1]
actions.consequence: No focused trigger or recurrence-risk information is obtained.
answerKeywords: delay care for a full history

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the focused history
actions.feedback: State which event, medication and recurrence-risk details are needed before disposition. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No additional history is obtained; disposition risk remains incompletely characterized.

steps.prompt: What ongoing care and disposition are appropriate after the initial response?
steps.guidance: Consider whether recovery is sustained, whether the patient can eat safely, what caused the event and how the medication plan will be reviewed.

actions.text: Continue observation, offer food or longer-acting carbohydrate when safe, and review the insulin plan and follow-up before considering discharge
actions.feedback: Do not discharge on one improved reading alone. Confirm sustained clinical and glucose recovery, safe intake, a plan for the missed-meal trigger and appropriate diabetes follow-up under local guidance. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The patient remains under observation while sustained recovery and a safe follow-up plan are confirmed.

actions.text: Discharge immediately after one improved glucose result without reviewing the cause or plan
actions.feedback: One improved reading does not establish sustained recovery or a safe medication plan. Continue observation and address the precipitating missed meal and follow-up. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient leaves after the first repeat measurement without further observation or review.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the disposition plan
actions.feedback: State how sustained recovery, safe intake, the cause and follow-up will be reviewed before discharge is considered. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No disposition change is made; the patient remains under observation.

endOfCaseSummary.diagnosis: Acute symptomatic hypoglycemia in an adult with diabetes
endOfCaseSummary.summary: Fictional beginner case: a missed meal after the usual mealtime insulin is associated with symptomatic level 2 hypoglycemia. The patient is cooperative and demonstrates safe swallowing, allowing oral carbohydrate treatment. It is an educational example, not a prescribing protocol.
endOfCaseSummary.idealApproach: Perform ABCDE assessment, check bedside glucose promptly, establish safe swallowing, give oral glucose-containing carbohydrate, objectively reassess glucose and mental status, then take a focused history. Continue observation, ensure safe intake, address the missed-meal trigger and review the regimen and follow-up before discharge is considered. If glucose measurement or treatment was deferred for routine imaging or a full history, an immediate reversible threat was not prioritized. If reassessment or follow-up review was omitted, compare your sequence with the need to establish sustained recovery.
endOfCaseSummary.disposition: Continue observation, provide food or longer-acting carbohydrate when safe, and confirm sustained clinical and glucose recovery. Review the precipitating missed meal, medication plan and diabetes follow-up with the supervising clinician; consider discharge only when safe under local guidance.
learningPoints: Prioritize ABCDE assessment and a rapid bedside glucose measurement; do not delay correction for non-urgent history or imaging.
Choose oral carbohydrate only after the patient is cooperative and swallowing safely; severe altered consciousness requires a non-oral route and urgent escalation.
Repeat glucose and reassess mental status after treatment; sulfonylurea exposure and renal impairment increase concern for recurrence or prolonged hypoglycemia.

cases.title: Reduced responsiveness after unplanned activity
learningObjectives: Recognize common clinical features of acute hypoglycemia and confirm it with a bedside measurement.
Prioritize emergency assessment and select a treatment route that matches the patient’s ability to swallow safely.
Reassess the clinical and glucose response, identify recurrence risk and plan an appropriate disposition.

criticalActionGroups.label: Correct the low glucose using a route appropriate to the examination

demographics.context: Brought to the ED by a family member after becoming difficult to rouse following a long walk.

initialPresentation.complaint: Marked drowsiness after prolonged activity and limited food intake.
initialPresentation.appearance: Severely drowsy and unable to cooperate with oral intake; airway is patent with positioning.
initialPresentation.condition: Reduced responsiveness with no safe oral route established.

steps.prompt: A patient with an acute change in behavior and sweating arrives at the ED. What should happen first?
steps.guidance: Start with immediate threats and reversible causes. Which rapid assessment can establish stability before non-urgent tasks?

actions.text: Perform an immediate ABCDE assessment and summon senior help for severe altered consciousness
actions.feedback: ABCDE assessment identifies immediate airway and breathing needs; severe altered consciousness warrants prompt senior help. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: A rapid primary assessment is underway; immediate threats are addressed before non-urgent tasks.

patientChanges.condition: Severely drowsy; airway is patent with positioning while immediate assessment and senior support proceed.

actions.text: Wait without assessment or treatment
actions.feedback: An acute change in mental status can reflect a rapidly reversible emergency. Do not delay ABCDE assessment and bedside glucose for a full history or routine imaging. [R1]
actions.consequence: No primary assessment or corrective treatment has started; the patient remains symptomatic.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the immediate plan
actions.feedback: No specific immediate action was identified. State an actionable primary assessment before non-urgent tasks. [R1]
actions.consequence: No new assessment or treatment is started; the patient remains in the current condition.

steps.prompt: The primary assessment is underway. Which immediately available result could change what you do next?
steps.guidance: Choose a rapid bedside investigation for a reversible cause of altered behavior. Avoid tests that do not address the immediate threat.

actions.text: Check a bedside capillary glucose
actions.feedback: The measured glucose of 1.8 mmol/L is below the hypoglycemia alert threshold and requires prompt correction; do not delay treatment for a laboratory confirmation. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The bedside meter returns an immediate result.

actions.text: Arrange routine head CT before checking bedside glucose
actions.feedback: There is no trauma or focal finding in the initial presentation to justify delaying a rapid glucose check. If symptoms persist after correction or new findings emerge, assess for other causes. [R1]
actions.consequence: No new glucose result is available; the patient remains symptomatic.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the investigation plan
actions.feedback: No specific immediate investigation was identified. State which bedside result could rapidly change care. [R1]
actions.consequence: No new investigation result is available; the patient remains in the current condition.

steps.prompt: The low bedside glucose is confirmed. What focused examination finding is needed before choosing a treatment route?
steps.guidance: Treatment safety depends on current mental status and ability to protect the airway and swallow, not simply on whether the patient is awake.

actions.text: Assess airway, mental status and ability to swallow safely
actions.feedback: The examination establishes whether oral treatment is safe and whether airway support or a parenteral route is needed. Being awake alone does not establish safe swallowing. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: A focused airway, neurologic and swallow-safety assessment is completed.

reveals.label: Focused findings
reveals.text: Airway remains patent with positioning. The patient cannot follow commands or safely swallow; no seizure, trauma or focal neurological deficit is found.

actions.text: Assume swallowing is safe because the patient is breathing
actions.feedback: Reduced responsiveness and inability to follow commands make oral treatment unsafe; bypassing this check risks aspiration. Establish the airway and use an appropriate non-oral route. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: Swallow safety has not been established; no examination result is available.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the examination plan
actions.feedback: No focused examination was identified. State how airway, mental status and swallow safety will be assessed before choosing a route. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No new examination finding is available; the patient remains in the current condition.

steps.prompt: The examination and glucose result are available. What treatment should be started now?
steps.guidance: Treat promptly with a route that is safe for the demonstrated level of consciousness and swallowing ability. Plan an objective reassessment.

actions.text: Give IV glucose promptly and summon senior help according to local protocol
actions.feedback: The patient is unable to swallow safely. IV glucose is preferred when access is available; severe altered consciousness also needs urgent senior support. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: Parenteral glucose is administered while airway status and senior support are maintained; no repeat measurement is available yet.

patientChanges.condition: Severely drowsy; airway positioning and close observation continue during treatment.

actions.text: If IV access is not immediately available, give IM glucagon while obtaining access and urgent help
actions.feedback: IM glucagon is an alternative when IV access is unavailable, but it may be less effective with sulfonylurea exposure. Continue urgent access, senior support and reassessment rather than waiting on glucagon alone. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: IM glucagon is given while IV access and senior support are pursued; no repeat measurement is available yet.

patientChanges.condition: Severely drowsy; close airway observation continues while glucose treatment takes effect.

synonyms: glucagon if IV access is unavailable

actions.text: Give oral glucose despite the patient being unable to swallow safely
actions.feedback: Do not put oral carbohydrate into the mouth of a patient who cannot cooperate or swallow safely; aspiration is a serious risk. Use a non-oral route and support the airway. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: Oral treatment cannot be safely administered; airway safety and immediate non-oral treatment are required.
synonyms: give oral glucose despite unsafe swallowing
give oral carbohydrate to an unconscious patient
attempt oral treatment without swallow safety

actions.text: Give additional insulin to treat the low glucose
actions.feedback: Additional insulin would lower glucose further and cannot treat hypoglycemia. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient remains severely drowsy and the glucose may fall further.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the treatment plan
actions.feedback: No specific treatment was identified. State a safe non-oral route and urgent escalation plan. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No corrective treatment is started; the patient remains severely drowsy.

steps.prompt: What should be checked after the initial treatment?
steps.guidance: Use both an objective glucose measurement and clinical response. A single improvement does not rule out recurrence.

actions.text: Repeat capillary glucose and reassess mental status after treatment
actions.feedback: A repeat bedside measurement and clinical reassessment confirm the initial response. Continue monitoring when the cause or medication profile creates recurrence risk. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The immediate glucose response is objectively checked.

reveals.label: Post-treatment reassessment
reveals.text: Glucose is 4.3 mmol/L (77 mg/dL). The patient opens eyes to voice, follows simple commands and can now protect the airway; ongoing fatigue remains.

patientChanges.condition: The patient opens eyes to voice, follows simple commands and can now protect the airway; ongoing fatigue remains.

actions.text: Assume correction because the patient looks better
actions.feedback: Symptom improvement alone is not enough to confirm biochemical correction. Repeat the glucose and reassess mental status. [R1, R2, R3]
actions.consequence: The treatment response is not yet objectively confirmed.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the reassessment plan
actions.feedback: No specific reassessment was identified. State which objective measurement and clinical findings should be checked. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No new reassessment result is available; the patient remains under care.

steps.prompt: The immediate glucose response is known. What focused history will help explain the event and guide ongoing care?
steps.guidance: Ask briefly about medication, food intake, activity, prior episodes, illness and factors that could make hypoglycemia recur.

actions.text: Ask about diabetes medicines, recent doses, food intake, activity, prior episodes and relevant illness or kidney disease
actions.feedback: A short, targeted history identifies the likely trigger and medication-related recurrence risk without replacing stabilization or objective reassessment. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient and companion provide focused information about the event and medication history.

reveals.label: Event and intake
reveals.text: A longer-than-usual walk was followed by very little food intake. The prescribed glucose-lowering medicine was taken as usual; no treatment was given before arrival.

reveals.label: Medication and recurrence factors
reveals.text: The patient took the usual prescribed sulfonylurea before a longer-than-usual walk and ate very little. A companion reports chronic kidney disease with a recent decline in renal function; no extra dose or intentional overdose is identified.

actions.text: Take a complete, non-targeted past history before identifying the event trigger
actions.feedback: Once immediate treatment and reassessment are underway, focus on the event, medicines, recent intake, activity and recurrence risks rather than allowing an unfocused interview to delay safe planning. [R1]
actions.consequence: No focused trigger or recurrence-risk information is obtained.
answerKeywords: delay care for a full history

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the focused history
actions.feedback: State which event, medication and recurrence-risk details are needed before disposition. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No additional history is obtained; disposition risk remains incompletely characterized.

steps.prompt: What ongoing care and disposition are appropriate after the initial response?
steps.guidance: Consider the severity of the episode and whether the medication and renal history creates risk of recurrent or prolonged hypoglycemia.

actions.text: Admit for monitored care, serial glucose checks and urgent senior or diabetes-team review of the sulfonylurea and renal impairment
actions.feedback: Severe hypoglycemia with sulfonylurea exposure and renal impairment can recur or persist after an initial correction. Do not discharge immediately; arrange monitored inpatient review. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: A monitored admission and senior medical review are arranged; glucose and mental status continue to be followed.

actions.text: Continue monitored ED care with serial glucose checks while urgently arranging senior review and admission
actions.feedback: This is a safe interim plan while the monitored inpatient setting is arranged; it is not a rationale for discharge after one normal result. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient remains in monitored ED care while senior review and admission are arranged.
synonyms: continue monitored ED care and arrange admission
escalate to senior and medical team for admission
monitored care while arranging inpatient review

actions.text: Discharge after the first improved glucose result without ongoing monitoring or medication review
actions.feedback: An initial response does not remove the risk of recurrent or prolonged hypoglycemia with a sulfonylurea and kidney impairment. Arrange ongoing monitored care and senior review. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: The patient leaves after a transient improvement without monitoring or recurrence-risk review.

actions.text: Continue current observation while clarifying the disposition plan
actions.feedback: State why the episode severity and medication/renal history require an explicit monitored-care and senior-review plan. [R1, R2]
actions.consequence: No disposition change is made; the patient remains under observation.

endOfCaseSummary.diagnosis: Acute symptomatic hypoglycemia in an adult with diabetes
endOfCaseSummary.summary: Fictional intermediate case: exercise and limited food are associated with severe hypoglycemia in a patient taking a sulfonylurea who has chronic kidney disease. Altered mental status requires third-party assistance (ADA level 3); impaired swallowing requires non-oral emergency treatment and monitored care. It is an educational example, not a prescribing protocol.
endOfCaseSummary.idealApproach: Perform ABCDE assessment and summon senior help, check bedside glucose promptly, establish airway and swallow safety, treat without an oral route, and repeat glucose and mental-status assessment. After stabilization, obtain focused collateral history. The combination of severe altered mental status, sulfonylurea exposure and renal impairment creates recurrence or prolonged-event risk; arrange monitored inpatient care and urgent medication review rather than discharge after an initial correction. If oral treatment was attempted without safe swallowing or monitoring was stopped after one improved result, compare your sequence with these risks.
endOfCaseSummary.disposition: Continue monitored care and arrange admission with urgent senior or diabetes-team review. Continue serial glucose and clinical monitoring and review sulfonylurea use and renal impairment; do not discharge after a transient initial correction.
learningPoints: Prioritize ABCDE assessment and a rapid bedside glucose measurement; do not delay correction for non-urgent history or imaging.
Choose oral carbohydrate only after the patient is cooperative and swallowing safely; severe altered consciousness requires a non-oral route and urgent escalation.
Repeat glucose and reassess mental status after treatment; sulfonylurea exposure and renal impairment increase concern for recurrence or prolonged hypoglycemia.
